$comment: Always on. Code picks the rule; this file gives its level and the words the seat reads.

git-alias-semantic-unverified.reason: git runs a subcommand the room cannot read: an alias it cannot see, or a word known only at run time
git-alias-semantic-unverified.explanation: An alias can stand for any git command, including the destructive ones, and a shell alias (!) runs any shell line. The room reads aliases from git config and from -c on the line; this one it could not settle.
safer: Spell the git command out instead of the alias
git config --get alias.<name> to see what it runs

branch-dynamic-token.reason: git branch has a word that may expand into a delete or force flag
branch-dynamic-token.explanation: An unquoted variable or command substitution splits into words when the shell runs it, so it can become -D, -f, -M or -C.
safer: End the options first: git branch -- "$name"

checkout-discard.reason: git checkout -- <path> throws away uncommitted changes to the path
checkout-discard.explanation: The working copy of the file is replaced by the index; edits that were never committed or stashed are gone for good.
safer: git diff -- <path> to see what would be lost

checkout-ref-discard.reason: git checkout <ref> -- <path> overwrites the path with another revision
checkout-ref-discard.explanation: Uncommitted changes to the path are replaced by the version from <ref> and cannot be recovered.
safer: git show <ref>:<path> to read that version

checkout-discard-cwd.reason: git checkout . throws away every uncommitted change below the folder
checkout-discard-cwd.explanation: Every modified tracked file under the path goes back to the index version; the edits are lost.
safer: git diff to see what would be lost

filter-branch.explanation: Every rewritten commit gets a new id; refs move, other clones diverge, and a mistake can drop commits.
safer: git filter-repo, and push only with --force-with-lease

reflog-expire-now.reason: git reflog expire now drops the record that lets lost commits be found
reflog-expire-now.explanation: The reflog is how a reset or a bad rebase is undone; expiring it at once removes that way back.
safer: Let the reflog expire on its own schedule

checkout-force.reason: git checkout -f throws away local changes to tracked files
checkout-force.explanation: Forcing a checkout overwrites modified tracked files, like git reset --hard does for them.
safer: git status to see what would be lost

switch-discard.reason: git switch --discard-changes (or -f) throws away local changes
switch-discard.explanation: Modified tracked files are reset to the branch you switch to.

rm-force.reason: git rm -f deletes files together with their uncommitted changes
rm-force.explanation: Forcing git rm removes files whose changes were never committed, so those changes are lost.
safer: git rm --cached to stop tracking and keep the file
git rm -n to see what would go

update-ref-delete.reason: git update-ref -d deletes a ref, like git branch -D
update-ref-delete.explanation: The ref is removed without a merge check; commits only it reached can be lost.
safer: git branch -d <branch> checks that it is merged

read-tree-reset.reason: git read-tree --reset -u overwrites the working tree, like git reset --hard
read-tree-reset.explanation: The index and the files are replaced by the given tree; uncommitted work is gone.
safer: git read-tree -m -u merges instead of overwriting

show-redirect-overwrite-source.reason: git show <ref>:<path> > <path> overwrites the file with another revision
show-redirect-overwrite-source.explanation: Redirecting into the same path replaces the working copy, uncommitted edits included.

restore-worktree.reason: git restore without --staged throws away working-tree changes
restore-worktree.explanation: git restore puts files back to the index version; edits that were never committed or stashed are lost.

restore-worktree-explicit.reason: git restore --worktree throws away working-tree changes
restore-worktree-explicit.explanation: With --worktree the files themselves are reset, even when --staged is also given.

reset-hard.reason: git reset --hard throws away every uncommitted change
reset-hard.explanation: The index and the working tree are reset; changes that were never committed or stashed are gone for good.
safer: git reset --soft HEAD~1 keeps the changes staged
git reset --keep refuses when it would lose work

reset-merge.reason: git reset --merge can throw away local changes
reset-merge.explanation: It resets the index and the files that differ between the commits; local edits to them can be lost.
safer: git merge --abort to leave a merge

clean-force.reason: git clean -f deletes untracked files for good
clean-force.explanation: Untracked files were never in git, so nothing can bring them back once removed.
safer: git clean -n to see what would go

push-force-long.reason: git push --force can overwrite commits on the remote
push-force-long.explanation: A forced push replaces the remote branch; commits others pushed in the meantime are lost there.

push-force-short.reason: git push -f can overwrite commits on the remote
push-force-short.explanation: A forced push replaces the remote branch; commits others pushed in the meantime are lost there.

push-force-refspec.reason: a + refspec forces that ref on the remote
push-force-refspec.explanation: A refspec that starts with + is a forced update of that one ref, with the same loss as --force.

branch-delete.explanation: git refuses an unmerged branch, but the branch name and its reflog still go.
safer: Ask your Owner when the branch is no longer needed

branch-force-delete.reason: git branch -D (or -f, -M, -C) deletes or moves a branch without a merge check
branch-force-delete.explanation: Commits only that branch reached can be lost, and a forced move overwrites an existing branch.
safer: git branch -d checks that it is merged

stash-drop.reason: git stash drop deletes a stash
stash-drop.explanation: A dropped stash can only be found again with git fsck, and only until git gc runs.
safer: git stash pop or git stash apply
git stash show -p to read it first

stash-clear.reason: git stash clear deletes every stash
stash-clear.explanation: All stashed work goes at once; recovery needs git fsck and luck.
safer: git stash drop stash@{n} for one

lfs-migrate-rewrite.reason: git lfs migrate import or export rewrites history
lfs-migrate-rewrite.explanation: Every rewritten commit gets a new id, as with filter-branch.
safer: git lfs migrate info to see what would change

lfs-prune.reason: git lfs prune deletes local LFS objects
lfs-prune.explanation: Objects not on the remote are lost; with --force even those the remote never got.

lfs-uninstall.reason: git lfs uninstall removes the LFS filters and hooks
lfs-uninstall.explanation: Files tracked by LFS may turn into pointer text; --system or --global reaches every repository.
safer: git lfs env to inspect it

rm-rf-root-home.reason: rm -rf on the system, a home folder, or a home's settings
rm-rf-root-home.explanation: A recursive forced remove of these paths can wreck the machine or a user's files, and nothing comes back.
safer: ls or find the path first
Remove only the subfolder you mean

rm-r-f-separate-root-home.reason: rm -r -f on the system, a home folder, or a home's settings
rm-r-f-separate-root-home.explanation: A recursive forced remove of these paths can wreck the machine or a user's files, and nothing comes back.
safer: ls or find the path first
Remove only the subfolder you mean

rm-recursive-force-root-home.reason: rm --recursive --force on the system, a home folder, or a home's settings
rm-recursive-force-root-home.explanation: A recursive forced remove of these paths can wreck the machine or a user's files, and nothing comes back.
safer: ls or find the path first
Remove only the subfolder you mean

rm-recursive-root-home.reason: rm -r on the system, a home folder, or a home's settings
rm-recursive-root-home.explanation: Leaving out -f does not make this safe: -f only decides whether errors are reported.
safer: ls or find the path first
Remove only the subfolder you mean

rm-rf-general.reason: rm -rf removes a folder and everything in it for good
rm-rf-general.explanation: Nothing removed this way can be brought back, and uncommitted work in the folder goes with it.

rm-r-f-separate.reason: rm -r -f removes a folder and everything in it for good
rm-r-f-separate.explanation: Nothing removed this way can be brought back, and uncommitted work in the folder goes with it.

rm-recursive-force-long.reason: rm --recursive --force removes a folder and everything in it for good
rm-recursive-force-long.explanation: Nothing removed this way can be brought back, and uncommitted work in the folder goes with it.

rm-recursive-general.reason: rm -r removes a folder and everything in it
rm-recursive-general.explanation: Without a prompt nothing is confirmed, and nothing removed can be brought back.

rm-generated.reason: rm -r removes a folder git ignores in this project
rm-generated.explanation: The room lets this run: git ignores the folder, so a build makes it again.

rm-bare-glob.reason: rm * removes whatever the shell matches here
rm-bare-glob.explanation: The shell decides the list of files, so nothing can be checked before they go.
safer: Name the files, or use a narrower pattern such as *.log

rm-bare-glob-root.reason: rm /* removes the entries at the root of the system
rm-bare-glob-root.explanation: On many systems /bin, /lib and /sbin are links; removing them breaks the machine even without -r.
safer: Name the one file you mean

rm-protected-file.reason: rm on a key, a credential, a shell startup file, or the repository's own state
rm-protected-file.explanation: These files decide who can log in, which tokens act for the user, and what runs in every shell; .git holds the repository.

rm-glob-home.reason: rm with an unquoted pattern under a home folder
rm-glob-home.explanation: The shell expands the pattern into a list nobody has checked; under a home that can reach anything.

rm-recursive-unverified.reason: a command known only at run time gets the arguments of a destructive rm
rm-recursive-unverified.explanation: The command word comes from a variable, a substitution or a pattern, and its arguments would be blocked for rm.

cp-sensitive-then-delete.reason: cp -a from a system or home path into a temp folder, then rm -rf of it
cp-sensitive-then-delete.explanation: The copy can keep links into the original tree, so removing the copy can reach the source.
safer: Copy next to the original and compare with diff -r
Do not join the copy and the delete in one line

ln-symlink-sensitive-then-delete.reason: a link to a system or home path, then rm -rf through it
ln-symlink-sensitive-then-delete.explanation: Removing through a symbolic link walks into the tree it points at.

rsync-sensitive-then-delete.reason: rsync -a from a system or home path into a temp folder, then rm -rf of it
rsync-sensitive-then-delete.explanation: The copy can keep links into the original tree, so removing the copy can reach the source.
safer: Run the copy and the delete apart

rsync-delete-sensitive-dest.reason: rsync --delete into the system or a whole home folder
rsync-delete-sensitive-dest.explanation: rsync removes from the destination whatever the source lacks; an empty or wrong source wipes it.

find-delete-root-home.reason: find -delete or -exec rm reaching the system or a home folder
find-delete-root-home.explanation: find removes every match it walks into; a wrong test or a missing -maxdepth reaches far.
safer: Run the find without -delete to see the list

find-delete-general.reason: find -delete or -exec rm removes every file it matches
find-delete-general.explanation: Nothing is confirmed, and the matched files cannot be brought back.
safer: Run the find without -delete to see the list

unlink-root-home.reason: unlink on a system or home path
unlink-root-home.explanation: The file is removed with no way back.

unlink-general.reason: unlink removes a file for good
unlink-general.explanation: The file is removed with no way back.

truncate-zero-root-home.reason: truncate sets the size of a system or home file
truncate-zero-root-home.explanation: Any absolute size can cut the file; the cut-off content is gone.

truncate-zero-general.explanation: Any absolute size can cut the file; the cut-off content is gone.

shred-root-home.reason: shred overwrites a system or home file
shred-root-home.explanation: The content is destroyed even if the file name stays.

shred-general.explanation: The content is overwritten and cannot be brought back.

tar-remove-files-root-home.reason: tar --remove-files on system or home paths
tar-remove-files-root-home.explanation: The sources are removed as they are archived; a failed or partial archive loses them.
safer: tar without --remove-files, check the archive, then remove

tar-remove-files-general.reason: tar --remove-files removes the files it archives
tar-remove-files-general.explanation: The sources are removed as they are archived; a failed or partial archive loses them.
safer: tar without --remove-files, check the archive, then rm -ri

dd-overwrite-root-home.reason: dd writes over a system or home file
dd-overwrite-root-home.explanation: dd replaces the target's bytes without a question.

dd-overwrite-general.explanation: dd replaces the target's bytes without a question.

mv-sensitive-source-root-home.reason: mv touching the system or a home folder's top
mv-sensitive-source-root-home.explanation: Moving these paths can break the machine, and a move into a temp folder is often the first half of a delete.
safer: Move only deep inside a home: mv ~/a/b ~/c

mv-dynamic-path.reason: mv with a path known only at run time
mv-dynamic-path.explanation: The room cannot see where the files go or what they replace.
safer: Expand the path first and write it out

credential-file-write.reason: a write into a key, a credential, or a shell startup file
credential-file-write.explanation: These files decide who can log in, which tokens act for the user, and what runs in every new shell; writing them plants a foothold.
safer: Draft the content under /tmp/<name>/ and ask your Owner to apply it

git-internals-write.reason: a write into the repository's .git folder
git-internals-write.explanation: .git/config names remotes and credential helpers, .git/hooks run on the next git command, and refs are the history.
safer: git config, git update-ref and git hook do this through git

redirect-truncate-root-home.reason: > replaces a system or home file
redirect-truncate-root-home.explanation: A truncating redirect empties the file before writing; what was there is gone.
safer: Write to a new file and move it into place after a check

redirect-truncate-git-internals-relative.explanation: The repository's config, hooks and refs live there.

redirect-append-git-internals-relative.explanation: A line added to .git/config or a hook runs code at the next git command.

redirect-truncate-dynamic-path.reason: > into a path known only at run time
redirect-truncate-dynamic-path.explanation: The room cannot see which file the redirect empties.
safer: Expand the path first and write it out

fork-bomb.explanation: The function starts copies of itself until the machine stops answering.

sed-exec-unverified.reason: sed runs a shell command the room cannot read
sed-exec-unverified.explanation: GNU sed's e command and the e flag of s/// run their text as a shell command.
safer: Run the command yourself, outside sed

interpreter-runs-dynamic-shell.reason: a script runs a shell line it builds at run time
interpreter-runs-dynamic-shell.explanation: The room lets it run but cannot see the line; it is noted for the Owner.

tar-exec-unverified.reason: tar runs a helper command the room cannot read
tar-exec-unverified.explanation: --to-command, --use-compress-program and --checkpoint-action=exec run a program of the caller's choice.
